bp: A citation network is a map of scientific work: papers point to papers, authors write papers, venues host papers, and institutions place researchers in communities. People use that map to find related researchers, group authors by research area, and trace where ideas travel. The trouble is that the map often has thin labels. A citation link says one paper cites another, but it may not say much about what the venue represents, what an affiliation implies, or what missing keywords should have signaled. This paper asks whether large language models, meaning text systems trained to produce plausible explanations from written context, can add useful factual descriptions to sparse citation metadata. The goal is not to replace citations with prose. It is to make the existing graph more informative, so downstream tasks such as author classification and author clustering can see both the relationship structure and richer descriptions of the objects inside it.
wh: The hard part is that citation metadata is both connected and uneven. One author may have a clear affiliation, many papers, and good keywords; another may appear with a short or missing record. If a system treats all missing fields as empty, it mistakes lack of metadata for lack of meaning. But filling the blanks automatically is risky. A language model can produce a fluent sentence that sounds factual while adding something the record never supported. In a scientific citation network, that is especially dangerous because one invented affiliation or research area can change how authors are grouped. The network is also heterogeneous, meaning it contains different kinds of nodes such as authors, venues, keywords, and papers. A useful feature for one kind of node may not mean the same thing for another. The problem is therefore a balance: add context where metadata is sparse, but avoid turning uncertain guesses into confident graph evidence.
naive: A smart beginner would first keep the citation network as it is: use paper titles, available keywords, venue names, author affiliations, and citation links, then train a classifier or clustering method on those fields. When a field is missing, the beginner might leave it blank or use a simple hand-written feature such as the raw venue name. That fails because sparse fields create weak nodes. Two authors working in the same area may look unrelated if their metadata is incomplete, while two authors at similarly named venues may look related for the wrong reason. Another beginner move would be to ask a language model to fill every blank directly. That fails in the opposite direction: the model may supply plausible but unsupported facts, and the graph will then spread those mistakes through later author grouping.
ap: The paper's central move is to use language models as controlled context builders for sparse citation metadata, then feed the resulting descriptions into the network as features. Instead of asking the graph model to learn from bare keywords, venue strings, and affiliation fragments, the method asks a language model to produce concise factual descriptions for those fields. Those descriptions are then encoded with DeBERTa, a language model used here to turn text into compact numerical descriptions that a graph method can consume. The enriched descriptions become node features inside a heterogeneous citation network. The paper also treats hallucination as a first-class danger. It uses Chain-of-Thought-based prompting, meaning prompts that encourage stepwise reasoning before the final answer, and it evaluates the quality of the generated context. The practical idea is simple: let the language model expand thin labels, but inspect and structure that expansion before it influences classification and clustering.
mech: The mechanism begins with citation metadata and a citation network. The input includes connected scholarly objects: papers cite papers, authors attach to papers, venues publish papers, and metadata fields such as keywords, venues, and affiliations describe some of those objects. The method first finds fields that are sparse or too short to carry much meaning. For those fields, it uses a large language model such as GPT or Llama to write concise factual descriptions. A venue name, for example, can be turned into a short description of what kind of scholarly venue it is; an affiliation can be described in a way that gives more context than a raw string. The prompting is designed to reduce unsupported invention by asking for reasoned construction rather than a bare completion. Next, each generated description is passed through DeBERTa. In plain terms, DeBERTa reads the sentence and converts it into a fixed bundle of numbers whose distances and directions preserve useful textual similarities. Those bundles become node features in the heterogeneous citation network. The graph now has both edges, which say how objects are connected, and enriched node features, which say more about what each object is. Finally, downstream models use this knowledge-enriched network for author classification and author clustering, and the paper compares the results with traditional feature engineering methods.
math: The main mathematical object is a graph: a set of nodes joined by links. Here the nodes are not all the same kind. Some represent authors, some papers, some venues, and some metadata objects, so the graph must preserve type as well as connection. A link is a claim that two objects should inform each other, such as an author writing a paper or a paper appearing at a venue. The second object is a text-to-number representation. A generated description is too raw for a classifier, so DeBERTa compresses the sentence into numbers. That compression is useful only if nearby number bundles tend to mean similar descriptions. The method then combines two kinds of evidence: graph structure, which says who is connected, and textual features, which say what the connected objects appear to mean. The tradeoff is compression versus detail. Turning prose into numbers makes learning possible, but it hides the exact words and can blur distinctions. Another tradeoff is signal versus fabrication. Generated context can reveal information implicit in metadata, but if the generated text is wrong, the numerical feature gives the graph a clean-looking false clue. Chain-of-Thought prompting is a control mechanism: it tries to make generation follow a more checkable path before the feature is created.
dots: This paper sits where three recurring conference ideas meet. It belongs to graph learning because the final object is still a network, and the point is to let connected scholarly objects carry evidence to author classification and clustering. It belongs to knowledge-graph and citation-network work because the useful facts are structured: authors, papers, venues, keywords, and affiliations are different kinds of entities with different relationships. It also belongs to the large-language-model thread because the missing signal is created from text generation rather than from manual feature rules. Neighboring papers in the repo show the same pressure in other settings: conversational entity retrieval uses graph neighborhoods to find the right knowledge-graph entity, while LLM-enhanced graph work uses language models to add semantic descriptions to nodes whose raw labels are too thin. The shared problem is sparse evidence. This paper's answer is to enrich the labels first, then let the network use both links and descriptions.
ww: The method should help when sparse metadata hides real similarity. Suppose two authors work in related areas but their available records contain different surface clues: one has good keywords, the other has an affiliation or venue that indirectly signals the same community. A bare network may not connect them strongly enough. Generated factual descriptions can turn those indirect clues into more comparable language, and DeBERTa can then place the descriptions into numerical features that make related nodes easier to group. The graph step matters because an author is not defined only by one sentence; the author is surrounded by papers, venues, and citation patterns. When richer node features are attached to that surrounding structure, classification and clustering have more evidence than either text or links alone. This improves over hand-written features because the system is not limited to a small set of manually chosen cues. It improves over blind generation because the generated context is targeted at sparse metadata fields and paired with evaluation for quality. The abstract's reported gains in author classification and clustering are consistent with this mechanism.
po: The payoff is a richer citation network that is better at organizing researchers. The abstract reports that the LLM-powered context augmentation improves author classification by 2.0% to 4.5% and author clustering by 8.9% to 18.1%, outperforming traditional feature engineering methods. In practical terms, this means a scholarly search or analysis system can group authors and research communities more accurately when the original metadata is incomplete. The paper also contributes a reusable direction: use language models not only to answer questions, but to add carefully generated context to structured scientific data. The dataset and source code are reported as available, which helps others inspect and reuse the construction pipeline.
limits: The method depends on the generated descriptions being mostly factual. If the language model invents venue meanings, affiliation details, or keyword context, the graph can treat false statements as strong evidence. Chain-of-Thought prompting and quality evaluation reduce this risk but do not prove that every generated feature is correct. The abstract also does not specify how performance changes across fields with different levels of sparsity, or whether the same gains hold outside the studied citation data. DeBERTa's numerical compression may miss fine distinctions between research areas that sound similar in prose. Finally, better author classification and clustering show useful downstream signal, but they do not by themselves prove that every enriched node is semantically faithful to the original metadata.
